title: “UX will be degraded until metrics improve” went viral
summary:
Twitter broke thread-loading in Nov 2019 and @visakanv basically snapped: first the rage-posts (“I really fucking hate it… it’s completely broken my experience”), then the heartbreak (“somebody just came into my personal library… and rampaged through it”), and then the cleanest possible slogan dropped like a hammer: **“THE USER EXPERIENCE WILL BE DEGRADED UNTIL METRICS IMPROVE.”** Trigger → meme: Twitter “optimizing for replies by breaking threads” leads to everyone replying out of sequence, which *creates more replies*, which Twitter can point at as “success.”

Peak was the line turning into a plug-and-play diagnosis for everything people already hated but couldn’t summarize. @QiaochuYuan uses it to explain Quora’s descent (“why were they so bad at filtering questions”), then later to scream about Spotify’s uneditable playlist columns (“cannot imagine the state of mind of the motherfucker at spotify…”). @Malcolm_Ocean turns it into a whole design philosophy rant—“billions… to hack peoples’ brains to make metrics go up. Design by proxy”—and applies it to Slack’s favicon red-dot chaos. @sharanvkaur keeps dropping it on every new “dark pattern” indignity (Twitter forcing phone numbers to unsubscribe, websites torching themselves to push apps) and even tries to mash it up with Singapore’s “displace, destroy, replace” urban-planning vibe.

Outcome/current state: the thread drama dies, but the sentence becomes a **sticky incantation**—@danielbrottman calls it “evergreen,” @visakanv literally hotkeys it as `uxdegraded`, and by 2025 he’s still quoting it when X swaps Communities for “xtok.” The residue is the shared vocabulary: whenever a product gets worse in a way that suspiciously helps engagement/upsells/ads, people don’t argue the specifics—they just drop the line and everyone immediately knows what kind of rot we’re talking about.
